blocks.text: Searching uses this global invariant. If the target is smaller than the current key, no key in the right subtree can match. If it is larger, the left subtree is excluded. It is the minimum of the right subtree. Why retain a temporary owner during replacement? It keeps the victim alive while retained child ownership is transferred. Why compare all keys after deletion? Absence of the target alone does not prove preservation of unrelated data. Why does a sorted snapshot not prove good performance? It says nothing about height.

reading.title: Guided lab — Validate whole-subtree ordering
paragraphs: Add a diagnostic validator using optional lower and upper integer bounds. Do not reuse contains as the validator: a search can miss exactly the keys misplaced by a broken invariant. Recompute the constraints from the root and inspect every node.

Create fixed deletion fixtures for a leaf, a root with one left child, a root with one right child, an immediate successor, a deep successor, and a successor with a right child. For each fixture, compare the complete remaining key set and verify that deleting the same key again returns false.

Add duplicate-heavy histories and a repeated empty-reuse cycle. Keep a vector of operations so a generated failure can be replayed exactly. When a failure occurs, shorten the history while preserving it; a minimal sequence often exposes one incorrect structural transition more clearly than thousands of preceding operations.

Instrument comparisons for sorted and shuffled insertion orders containing the same distinct keys. Report total insertion comparisons and final height. Do not use wall-clock time yet. Explain why identical in-order outputs can coexist with different search costs and recursion depths.

For an interface-design exercise, imagine nodes store records with stable external identifiers and mutable metadata. Decide whether copying a successor payload into another node is allowed under your identity promise. If callers retain node handles, document what deletion changes.
